one_liner: Rust Wasm interpreter using tail-call threaded code; about 1.1x faster than WAMR fast-interp in wasmi-benchmarks (bug-fixed fork measured).
what_it_does: Embeddable WebAssembly interpreter written in Rust with zero non-dev dependencies and about 15k lines. The API mirrors Wasmtime/Wasmi (Engine, Store, Module, Linker, Func::wrap, Func::call), so porting a host from those runtimes is mechanical, but it is not a drop-in crate replacement. A small CLI (makepad-stitch <file> <func> [args]) is also provided.
how_it_is_fast: Each Wasm instruction is compiled into a sequence of 'threaded' Rust functions that all share one signature, so each handler ends with a sibling call (tail call) that LLVM turns into a jump. Six integer and two float values (ip, sp, memory base and size, an integer and two float accumulators) are passed as arguments, which keeps the hot interpreter state in hardware registers; on Windows it forces the sysv64 ABI to get enough argument registers. Functions are compiled lazily on first call, and many specialised variants per instruction trade instruction-cache pressure for fewer stack moves.
when_to_use: A pure-Rust, dependency-free Wasm interpreter on 64-bit macOS, Linux or Windows where JIT is not allowed and fast build times matter (README: 2.29 s build vs 15.61 s Wasmi and 81 s Wasmtime on M2 Pro).
Compute-heavy MVP Wasm modules (no SIMD, no tail calls) where an interpreter within about 10% of WAMR fast-interp and Wasm3 is acceptable.
Experiments with tail-call threaded interpreter design in Rust; the executor and compiler are compact enough to read.
Hosts that already have a Wasmtime-style embedding and want an interpreter fallback with a similar API shape.
when_not_to_use: Anything correctness-critical: upstream issues #3 and #4 (open since July 2025 and June 2026) show live locals and stack registers not preserved on entering block/if/loop, so valid modules return wrong values; the fixes exist only in the Robbepop/stitch v0.1-dev fork.

If you want the fastest Rust interpreter: in the same wasmi-benchmarks run Wasmi v2 (x12.40) and Silverfir-nano (x9.02) beat Stitch (x15.73) on AMD EPYC 7763; Stitch trails Wasmi v2 by about 1.26x over the 20 cases it runs (derived from page data).

Large or modern modules: function bodies over 128 KiB, data segments over 1 MB and more than one memory are rejected at HEAD (src/config.rs), and SIMD, WASI, tail calls and the BigInt proposal are unsupported; FFmpeg is reported not to load (issue #1).
32-bit targets, Miri or any build where LLVM might not apply sibling-call optimisation; there is no trampoline fallback, so the interpreter would overflow the native stack.
Untrusted code with a strong safety requirement: large amounts of unaudited unsafe code (README).

integration.dependencies: none (criterion and wast are dev-dependencies only)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2021; HEAD uses size_of/align_of from the prelude, so Rust 1.80+ (inferred, not documented); release build required (debug profile set to opt-level 1)
integration.platforms: 64-bit only: x86-64 and aarch64 on macOS, Linux, Windows (README); no 32-bit
integration.thread_safety: Engine is Arc/Mutex-backed and cloneable across threads; execution needs &mut Store; host functions must be Send + Sync; Store Send/Sync not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — API shape is close to Wasmtime/Wasmi (Engine/Store/Linker/Func) but it is a different crate with fewer proposals and no WASI

gotchas: Open wrong-result bugs #3 and #4 (filed by the Wasmi author): e.g. a block with br_if returns 0 instead of 42. The wasmi-benchmarks numbers come from the Robbepop/stitch v0.1-dev fork (initial snapshot Sep 2025), which fixes #3/#4, raises the 128 KiB function-body limit and carries further fixes (memory.grow frame fixup, grow_with_stack, operand popping) whose presence at upstream HEAD was not confirmed; the published speed is for code that is not in makepad/stitch.
crates.io still serves makepad-stitch 0.1.0 from 2024-05-13 (2,521 downloads); repo HEAD (Nov 2025) is newer and unreleased, so `cargo install makepad-stitch` gets the old code.
Func::call without a caller-supplied Stack allocates a fresh zeroed 8 MiB stack per top-level call (src/func.rs); pass your own Stack for many short calls.

README CoreMark table compares against Wasmi 0.31.2 (now about 4x slower than Wasmi v2 in wasmi-benchmarks: x51.35 vs x12.40), and the Wasm3 runner is commented out of coremark/, so the Wasm3 column cannot be rerun from the repo.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over wasm3 or WAMR only when you need a pure-Rust, dependency-free interpreter with fast compile times and can live with roughly equal speed (1.04x over Wasm3, 1.10x over WAMR in wasmi-benchmarks); pick Wasmi v2 for a faster Rust interpreter with tail-call support, Silverfir-nano for the fastest interpreter in that suite, and wasm3 for 32-bit or microcontroller targets.
verified_claims_summary: Independent wasmi-benchmarks (criterion, AMD EPYC 7763, Aug 2026) measured the bug-fixed fork Robbepop/stitch v0.1-dev at a geomean of 15.73x the per-case fastest runtime, vs 16.51x Wasm3, 17.07x WAMR fast-interp, 27.92x Wasmtime Pulley and 12.40x Wasmi v2; the geomean covers the 18 of 21 execute cases every runtime ran (I reproduced all these values from the per-case plots). The first-party README CoreMark scores (Stitch 2950/1684/4592 vs Wasm3 2911/1734/3951 on M2 Pro/Xeon E312xx/i9-13900K) show Stitch roughly tied with Wasm3 on Mac and Linux and about 1.16x ahead on Windows.
status_note: Upstream makepad/stitch saw a cleanup burst in Nov 2025 but no response to four open issues including two wrong-result bugs; MIT and small enough to vendor, but treat it as experimental and prefer the Robbepop fork or Wasmi v2 for real use.
